title: ⚔️ Eryndor Living Atlas V — Factions, Mercenaries, Adventures & Gloin's Travel
rawNotionMarkup: New, playable Year 3,847 living-world encounter and travel layer. These factions, companies, campaigns, adventures and named NPCs are new setting additions developed to populate the pre-existing world. The famous Gloin/Borin/Hadrik/Maela/Edrik/Veyron plot and existing mysteries are not silently answered. Nothing written here advances Gloin's campaign clock or makes a future adventure inevitable. ## Enslavement and captivity in the grimdark layer — shared capacity across peoples The creator has established outright enslavers in Eryndor, including raids, coerced labor, sale of captives, corrupt state systems and cruel aristocratic exploitation. No people has an enslaver monopoly or a victim role by ancestry. Captors and captives can be members of the same intelligent species or different species. Motives vary: skills, money, war, revenge, dynastic prestige, political terror, ransom, debt, land and power. The Urakai warlord raiding a Khazari mining village for skilled labor is one non-canonical illustration and must not make the setting's established Urakai warlord a slave raider by assumption. Eryndor Living Atlas VII — Slavery, Bondage, Serfdom & Resistance records institutional distinctions, faction illustrations, political resistance, and the lived consequences. These are ongoing world threats where jurisdiction permits or law fails, not a scripted quest Gloin has accepted. ## Serious violence can occur in charming towns — newly reinforced tone The creator specifies that idyllic multi-species hamlets do not guarantee safety. Even a locally respected, physically formidable resident can unexpectedly turn violent, causing deaths or destruction and forcing a town guard, other residents or travelers to intervene; emergency lethal force is possible when necessary. No such incident is preordained for any named Ogre or other individual, and aggression is not a universal species trait. Realistic capacity, time to respond, casualties, trauma, legal consequences, rebuilt property and ruined trust persist. Eryndor Living Atlas VI — Patchwork Villages & Folktale Crossroads develops this at community level. Preserve Gloin's freedom to intervene, withdraw or ignore a rumor; do not manufacture automatic deadly encounters each time he visits a cozy town. ## Fantasy-scale demographics and consequences of mass upheaval — creator priority Explicit creator clarification: Eryndor's population and settlement scales should be larger and more ambitious than ordinary historical comparisons. The world contains long-established civilizations, immense cities, powerful armies, terrifying monsters, advanced and wondrous technologies, and magical phenomena. Great population centers make it possible for war, invasion, disease, siege, mass enslavement, ecological disasters and magical catastrophes to cause enormous losses of life, potentially reaching hundreds of thousands or more in an extreme regional or continental crisis. These possibilities are stakes, not preset body counts. Birth-rate freeze — explicit creator instruction: Do not alter, increase, accelerate or invent birth/fertility rates to justify large populations or to replace catastrophic losses. Preserve every already established species- and region-specific reproduction pattern. Where no numerical birth rate was previously set, leave it unquantified rather than guessing one. Long historical timescales, immigration, existing settlement patterns and fantasy-world scale can coexist with unchanged births; any post-catastrophe recovery takes real in-world time and may never fully occur. Larger possible casualty totals do not imply faster births. - Don't shrink existing numbers: The accepted population of Karak-Varn remains 3.8 million, with the established Khazari, Eldar and Urakai totals untouched. The new 343.8m atlas-wide numerical model is a provisional simulation baseline, not a cap on what fantasy-scale Eryndor may contain. Other populations can be revised or expanded at the owner's direction and as new regions are developed; do not invent a population revision now merely to support a hypothetical casualty. - Large losses have persistent aftermath: Count soldiers and civilians separately where possible. Missing people, prisoners, refugees, destroyed households, abandoned hamlets, orphaned children, injured survivors, displaced artisans, food shortages, changing tax bases and intergenerational resentment can reshape a realm. Historical institutions provide inspiration for recovery, relief, rebuilding, conscription and labor migration, but cannot prohibit extraordinary fantasy events. - Not every battle kills millions: An army may retreat, a siege may lift, a catastrophe may be prevented, an epidemic may be contained. Losses and outcomes depend on the actual scale, exposure, threats, preparation, decisions, magic and defenses. Avoid exaggerating ordinary skirmishes or making devastation inevitable just to prove Eryndor is grimdark. - Demographics change over time: If destruction actually occurs during play, update the affected region's residents, refugee flows, farming labor, reconstruction, military strength, inheritance and diplomacy. A civilization can have existed for millennia while enduring expansions, disasters, migrations and recovery rather than continuous unbroken growth. - Campaign safeguard: These are possible future consequences, not a claim that an unseen mass-casualty event has already happened. The world does not advance during the current Day 22 11:25 AM pause, and Gloin knows only what he could learn in-world. ## Operating principles of a genuine living world 1. Every major region has ordinary people, institutions, rivals and livelihoods, even if Gloin never visits. A miller can fail, a captain can retire, a convoy can succeed and a kingdom can negotiate peace offscreen when game time advances. 2. No universal adventurers' guild. Some towns host mercenary exchanges, guide associations, monster-bounty boards, explorer societies, courts and chartered expeditions; these differ in jurisdiction and customs. 3. Information is local. A road guide knows its county, a caravan master knows freight, a scholar knows texts, a soldier knows command. Gloin cannot read a private GM list as if it were public noticeboard knowledge. 4. Danger has an ecology and a cause. Starving predators, overgrazing, raiding companies, storms, lawless tolls, river floods and genuine monsters are all possible. No rule that every path leads back to the First Throne. 5. Contract realism: Pay, time, supplies, legal rights, liability for injury, baggage, taxes and return travel must be disclosed before a player accepts work. NPCs don't conjure food, maps or money from nothing. 6. Travel is a choice. Gloin may ignore any or all leads and can change professions. A quest offered is not a quest accepted. No made-up combat, income, skill gain or missed appointment until actual play. ## Regional political and civic institutions — new names with operating motives | Institution | Region and base | What it wants | Limits and genuine internal conflicts | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Seven Gates Freight Compact | Karak-Varn Deepway shippers | Predictable tolls, maintained shafts, mutual convoy credit | No power to order all seven independent kings; owners quarrel over private toll privileges | | Stone Ledger Surveyors | Az-Rhumen | Accurate maps, safe mines, paid certification | Competing scholarly schools and data ownership | | Westroad Teamsters | Copperspan–Staghollow | Dependable wagon freight and axle repairs | Price competition, theft and guild dues | | Greenbough Charter Council | Letharion | Balance managed timber, Ent grove rights and farmers' roads | Conservative foresters versus merchant road builders | | Silverflow Boatmasters | Western Avarra | River traffic, bridge safety and fair tolls | Floods, barge strikes and noble riparian rights | | Highmere Grain Ring | Aldermere | Stable harvest trade and lawful storage | Rumors of hoarding, farmers versus merchants | | Northwatch Quartermasters | Valtorian Marches | Provision a mobilizing frontier force | Pay arrears, political pressures and disputed authority | | Eastern Commons Council | Khurazh / eastern Urakai towns | Arbitration among autonomous clan markets | Rival road tariffs, emerging warlord reports; no pre-assigned secret allegiance | | Rider's Pasture Congress | Urakai/Centaur steppe markets | Mobility, safe wells and winter grazing | Settled farmers conflict with mobile herds | | Strait Pilot Brotherhood | Orrisport / Crown Sea | Licensed guides and naval charts | Rival republics, sea storms and unlicensed competition | | Blue Shell Envoys | Merfolk Shattered Isles | Reef protection, harbour exchange and fishing treaties | Different underwater cities have independent interests | | Worldbreak Supply Syndic | Skar Hold, Tharvorn | Winter grain stocks, timber and pass maintenance | Unreliable sponsors and winter transport risk | | Sahradi Water Recorders | Qasr Meradin | Accurate canals, water-rights registers and ration law | Factions favour different districts and rich estates | | Seven Rivers Lockwrights | Orundel river basin | Repair locks and dams, protect river transport | Dependence on city treasuries; ecological opposition | | Elderbough Grove Assembly | Vaelora Elderwood | Forest stewardship and negotiated livelihoods | Eldar, Ent, Satyr and human residents disagree | | Stormcairn Mutual | Vaelora ocean ports | Ship insurance and rescue | Merchant solvency, storm losses, insurance fraud | | Iron Circle Civil Trainers | Karak-Varn | Civilian readiness, paid lessons, military discipline | Not a Royal Army recruiting body by default; Keldrun's established course remains distinct | | Independent Road Healers | Cross-region itinerant | Tend to travellers, camps and accident victims | Professional standards, shortages and healer licensing | Named institutions here do not replace historical ones: Royal Mining Office, Royal Historical Archive, King Durgan IV's court, the existing guild networks, Maela's Silver Anvil, and the Concord of Crowns remain independent established entities. Veyron's motives are not retroactively resolved. ## Mercenary, escort and free-company register These are new groups that exist in the world as of the baseline date. They have ordinary recruitment and rivalries. Captain names are new NPCs. Members counted are a mix of veterans, support staff and trainees; a company of 90 does not field 90 heavily armored warriors every day. Rates are possible contract quotes, not income owed to Gloin. | Company / size | Base and commander | Reputation, speciality and likely work | Internal tension | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Bronze Lanterns / 84 | Copperspan, Captain Rysa Flintbraid (Khazari) | Reliable wagon escorts and mountain-road night watches; usually paid by convoy | Several injured veterans need pensions | | Blackstone Wardens / 140 | Stonewake Gate, Captain Garric Halfspade (Khazari) | Deepway gate patrol subcontractors, wagon protection and structural rescue | Heavy public suspicion of private gate guards | | Red Sash Company / 230 | Northwatch, Commander Elian Torf (human) | Veteran frontier infantry hired to fortify depots | Two officers disagree on serving expansionist campaigns | | Silver Stag Blades / 68 | Highmere, Captain Mera Hollowfield (human) | Village watches, escorting tax cargo, missing-person searches | Their wealthy patrons want preferential protection | | Eastwind Cords / 115 | Lanternreach, Captain Rukha Threestone (Urakai) | Caravan negotiation, cavalry scouts, Urakai/Khazari route escorts | Some members resent customs restrictions | | Blue Narrows Watch / 97 | Nacre Key, Captain Jessa Saltwake (Foxfolk) | Anti-piracy sail crew, salvage, port defence | Shares rescue profits unequally, inviting dissent | | Harrow Pike Veterans / 52 | Skeldhaven, Drogar Wolfmantle (Bearfolk) | Winter trail guards and mercenary river-sled security | Finances endangered by old contract debt | | Reedcross Lancers / 160 | Khurazh, Asha Kavrel (Centaur) | Steppe courier protection, cavalry-for-hire, bandit suppression | Clan pasture loyalties can override a foreign employer | | Golden Well Shields / 120 | Talasir, Samir Qadren (human) | Caravan water protection and oasis safety | Religious and clan neutrality requires compromise | | Broadgate Ward / 75 | Hornwell, Dovar Broadstep (Minotaur) | Fort construction, heavy haul rescue and caravan defensive duty | Slow-travel supply needs, expensive contracts | | Verdant Spears / 64 | Mangrove Crown, Selu Reedmark (Tigerfolk) | River scouts, flood rescue and jungle guide escorts | Refuse clear-cutting jobs; not universally beloved | | Lakeward Oars / 95 | Lakeharbor, Brenna Stillwake (Pigfolk) | Lakeboat security, rescue, barge dispute settlement | Low pay draws younger recruits away | | Black Gull Free Sailors / 190 | Orrisport, Captain Nellis Marr (human) | Maritime armed freight and sometimes legally ambiguous privateering | Letters of marque contested in three courts | | Riverhook Freelances / 35 | Seven Rivers Market, Vek Thornfin (Goblin) | Warehouse security, investigation of cargo loss and foot scouts | Members may exaggerate their local influence | | Emberguard Salvors / 43 | Emberback Gate, Tonn Kesra (Kobold) | Fire, collapse and steam-boiler salvage | Technical skill strong; inadequate medicine supplies | Recruitment principle: A company could take Gloin as a porter, novice guard, survey assistant or apprentice according to its actual current vacancies, aptitude, references, equipment and risk; no group automatically offers him a captain's commission. Where company size or race sounds unusual, that's a deliberate new setting design, not an indication the company appeared in the original campaign. ## Explorers, monster hunters and adventurers — distinct from military companies | Group | Base | Role, motives and complications | | --- | --- | --- | | Lantern Survey Fellowship | Karak-Varn / Copperspan | Cartographers, miners and scholarly guides; some missions purely bridge and tunnel surveying, not ancient ruins | | Wayfarer's Six | Orrisport | Independent adventuring party of six with a succession of contracts, quarrels and debts; not a universal quest guild | | Rook Feather Society | Elenvar | Botanical explorers, histories of forests and ancient sites; access by charter and etiquette | | Three Road Companions | Eastern Grasslands | Traveling three-person Urakai/halfling/Goblin team, specializing in remote deliveries and mediation | | Winter Cairn Seekers | Tharvorn | Small expedition society mapping summer glacier routes, sometimes rescuing stranded teams | | House of Falling Stars | Qasr Meradin | Independent observatory surveyors and scholars; research contested by institutions | | Riverward Inquiry | Veyrahn | Public-interest flood, canal, missing-barque and local corruption investigations | | Green Hollow Trackers | Vaelora | Wildlife protection and dangerous-predator response; not licensed to slaughter entire sentient communities | | The Long Road Kitchen | Cross-border travelling cooperative | Wagon-based cooks and medicine support working along disaster routes; their “adventures” are humanitarian logistics | | Glimmer Chisel Circle | Stonewake Gate | Gnomish/Kobold archaeological craft club, competitive, frequently more enthusiastic than safe | Monsters versus people: An Ogre clan or Harpy village is a sapient community with legal and individual agency. A mercenary notice about “kill all harpies” is a moral, political and tactical issue, not a world rule declaring an intelligent people exterminable. Some raiding bands really are dangerous, and the victims deserve protection; investigating who is responsible matters. ## Criminal networks, rumor brokers and lawful friction - Ragged Chain Cartel (Copperspan and western road): Organized cargo theft, fence shops, bribes and forged wagon passes. Not a world-spanning secret cult. Leader unknown publicly; financial stakes in legitimate repairs. - Fourth Lantern Smugglers (Shattered Coast): Avoid sea duties; some smuggle needed medicine, others dangerous contraband. Ship captains and port officials disagree about enforcement. - Grey-Toll Collectors (Aldermere–Valtoria march): Bandit group masquerading as official tax collectors. Threatened farmers may pay to survive; border patrols may actually pursue them. - Road-Cinder Crew (east Urakai caravan roads): Raiders recruit from dispossessed transport workers; sometimes attack mixed caravans. Do not imply they serve the unknown Urakai warlord without evidence. - Blue Scale Exchange (Sahrad): Money brokers and some counterfeiters trading in coin debasement, trade credit and fake water licenses. - Deep Salt Circle (Morn-Tar freight halls): Illegal toll bypass and black-market rationed salt; profit motive, not a First Throne conspiracy. - Forest-Saw League (Vaelora): Legally organized forestry lobby with a rogue illegal-logging wing. Not every logger is criminal and not every activist peaceful. ## Region-specific adventure and daily-life situations These are playable world situations, not confirmed completed quests, mandatory paths or guaranteed hidden-treasure spawns. A lead may be false, a client may refuse, another crew may resolve it first, or circumstances may change before Gloin arrives. ### Avarra: travel out of Karak-Varn 1. Three Lanterns bridge debt: A bridge repair has stopped coach service and two hamlet families cannot afford the assessment. Options include carpentry, negotiating with Copperspan toll officials, financing timber, or crossing at an unsafe ford. Consequences affect grain flow and local relationships. 2. Stonewake freight dispute: Freight weighers accuse merchants of evading gate duty; guards want witnesses. An apprentice surveyor can inspect weighing equipment, but forged documents complicate matters. 3. Missing Blackbell kiln hands: Several workers have not returned from a steam furnace repair. Could be preventable industrial injury, criminal negligence or unrelated desertion, not supernatural by default. 4. Staghollow harvest guard: Farmers face crop theft and wolf attacks, some of which may be ordinary wildlife, some connected to a stolen grain train. Escorting wagons, examining tracks or mediation are viable. 5. Crossing into Letharion: Forest-road guides disagree over an old cutting right that may violate an Ent grove agreement; local Eldar law matters. 6. Orik's ghost rumor: A tavern claims to have seen a vanished engineer near a foothill inn. Rumor can be false and is not a prewritten confirmation of his survival. 7. Western river ferry: Silverflow high water strands villages and increases price of flour; repair, lawful requisition or a detour matter. 8. Urakai well agreement: A Centaur herd and settled grain town contest a well; a mediator might prevent violence, but neither side will accept an outsider's word without grounds. 9. Northwatch supply trouble: A warehouse burns in a Valtorian frontier city; an honest investigator may uncover incompetence, arson or rumor, without requiring an invasion. 10. Shattered Isles reef rescue: A mixed crew is stranded; surface and Merfolk rescuers disagree about the salvage rights. ### Tharvorn 11. Frostford spring bridge: Water undermines the ferry pier; repair costs mean fishing families cannot move their catch. 12. Worldbreak winter route: A lost caravan's tracks lead toward a hazard; search-and-rescue without guaranteed recoveries. 13. Wolfsrest herd sickness: Veterinarian, feed and ranger diplomacy matter; do not turn disease into magic without evidence. 14. Brineglass shelf dispute: Surface fishing nets cross a Merfolk nursery, demanding restitution and treaty talks. 15. Rimecairn toll feud: A Troll village and nearby Human trading post dispute who maintains a bridge; folklore brands one side monstrous. ### Sahrad 16. Thirty Wells drought: Water escrow documents conflict, wealthy caravans get priority and poorer neighborhoods face shortages. 17. Hornwell supply contract: Minotaur quarry workers are owed wages by a Sultanate construction officer, and the walls cannot be repaired until settlement. 18. Keshan's Mouth fever season: Flood and poor water safety overwhelm healers; supply and sanitation choices matter. 19. Suncliff caravan raids: A dangerous Harpy band may be attacking pack animals; identify actual attackers without collective punishment. 20. Sandglass observatory: A miscopied lunar measurement threatens a scholar's reputation. Could lead to interesting astronomy without revealing the lost art of harmonisation. ### Orundel 21. Seven Rivers lock failure: A jammed river lock strands grain barges and threatens food prices. Engineers, Gnomish craftworkers and river pilots offer competing plans. 22. Ruzh-Tarek council vote: Two Urakai clans support different toll proposals; escorted witnesses and open political debate can change the outcome. 23. Emberback safety inspection: A steam pressure warning is dismissed by a busy mine owner. Professional testimony, labor organizing or law enforcement may intervene. 24. Mangrove Crown fever trade: A medicinal plant harvest could heal a local epidemic but violate jungle resource law. 25. Windhook beacon trouble: A cliffside signal line fails; aerial couriers compete with ground crews over pay and risk. ### Vaelora 26. Lakeharbor grain-loss mystery: Missing cargo could be spoilage, insurance fraud or theft, creating a genuine mercantile investigation. 27. Elderbough preservation hearing: Logging concession threatens ancient trees and farm jobs; no simple good-versus-evil solution. 28. Deepspring water rights: A Troll and Kobold waterworks cooperative is accused by a nearby city of over-diversion. 29. Stormcairn shipwreck season: Rescue ships need capable crew, an honest insurer and safe weather windows. 30. Willowhorn lost flock: A Satyr shepherd fears predators, while local scouts suspect a broken boundary gate; mundane possibility first. 31. Rootbound visitor: An Ent assembly permits a foreign scholar's hearing at a grove only if their foresters can show restraint and respect. 32. Crownwall road collapse: Khazari diaspora and human wagoners disagree over whose contract requires maintaining a mountain tunnel. Location-specific pay and risk: Put a fee on a contract only when a real employer, resources, scope and hazard are established. No free high-value quest rewards, no instant level-ups, and no automatically acquired ancient artifact. ## Gloin Hammerfeld: six realistic ways to leave Karak-Varn Current campaign reality: Autumn Day 22, Year 3,847, \~11:25 AM, Gloin is at the Royal Historical Archive with Maela at Hadrik's desk. Hadrik has asked what they uncovered. Gloin has not replied. Gloin is 42, healthy, not enlisted; last confirmed purse 10 silver and 82 copper, has personal axe, ordinary clothes and boots, keepsake, notebook, borrowed Hadrik volume. Borin holds the original nine-level survey. There is a Day 23 morning Keldrun training expectation and Bruni's promised metallurgy at 11:30 AM on Day 23; Maela's twice-weekly practical studies also exist, with exact future lesson schedule not all fixed. Elska's discreet natural/common magic research has been agreed but not begun, and Hadrik is not included unless the player chooses it. | Chosen direction, not a compulsory plot | First destination / estimated road travel from K-V | Money, companionship and world consequence | | --- | --- | --- | | West: the familiar trade road | Copperspan \~90 km; 3–5 days walking after reasonable meals and rest | Small jobs, Halfling farms, merchant wagon guarding and village disputes; Gloin may buy passage or walk | | East: the Urakai caravan frontier | Stonewake Gate \~45 km; 2–3 days on foot; Lanternreach \~215 km and more than a week | Customs and escorts, mixed cultures, cattle/grain trade; no inevitable war | | North: the mountain Thrones | Highbarrow \~125 km; 4–7 days on foot; longer into Thar-Keld | Mining, construction, winter road permits, independent royal laws | | South: industrial towns and heat roads | Underfall \~65 km; 2–4 days; Blackbell \~185 km | Engineering work, mining safety, forge politics and road contract | | West far: Letharion | Nine Oaks \~340 km; around 12–18 walking days plus forest clearance | Mixed villages and complex Eldar/Ent forest treaties; access not freely guaranteed | | Overseas eventually | First reach Shattered Coast or southern ports; cross via a named sailing route | Requires sea passage, food, funds, weather, ports, papers and time; no spontaneous cheap teleport | Planning estimate: Ordinary unescorted road walking in good conditions ≈ 20–30 km/day before fatigue and detours. Rural bed and food cost may consume roughly 10–20 copper/day or more depending on meals, accommodation, supplies and danger; prices are local estimates, not Gloin's automatic expenses. His purse is not unlimited, but he can reasonably undertake a modest trip without a noble's budget if he equips sensibly. Critical player choice: Gloin may answer Hadrik, reschedule or miss training commitments, tell Borin/Maela/family he plans to depart, seek a job, gather supplies and leave—in whatever order the player chooses. Do not assume he has already left, secretly notified them or broken an agreement. If he departs, relationships and missed commitments develop from realistic choices rather than punishing him by fiat. Neither the archive inquiry nor any unchosen training may hijack the travel story. ## Persistent people and world-turn procedure When Gloin arrives in a new settlement, the GM should silently prepare: 1. Municipality: named mayor/elder/council, population, resident people mix, legal system and local resource rights. 2. Livelihood: largest 3 trades, where food and water come from, what workers earn, who buys their exports. 3. Place: street/tunnel/bridge layout, district/smaller outlying hamlets, inn, market, shrine/school or analogous institution. 4. Human lives: at least 5 memorable recurring residents with independent motives, families and regular schedules; include mundane personalities and humor. 5. Factions: one local established institution, one genuine dispute, one external trade or political tie, and a reason not everyone agrees. 6. Encounter ecology: surrounding wildlife, season, local dangerous sites and which rumors are actually unproven. 7. Opportunities: 2 ordinary paid jobs, 1 social/historical lead and 1 situation that is not a quest at all. The player may ignore every one. 8. Memory: results become persistent ledger facts; merchants remember bargains, guards know arrests, children grow, a burned bridge stays burned until rebuilt. 9. Travel/narration: advance only actual elapsed in-world time, track meals and money if charged, and let distant events evolve without automatically giving Gloin global knowledge. 10. Audit: never replace source-established facts because a generator produces a different name or date. Stable settlement names, populations, maps and NPCs remain consistent unless there is an in-world reason for change. ## Backlog of still-unmapped material - Precise coastlines, river tributaries, town-by-town cartographic bearings beyond provisional reference grid, every hamlet in a world of 343.8m. - Exact named dynastic histories, populations of Drakari/Aelwyn, number of Living Mountains, every small people's biological lifespan and precise magical ecology. - Unresolved origins of lost Natural Magic harmonisation, earliest First Throne datings, the missing engineers and the actual truth beyond the sealed eastern mine. - Future direct original-chat sources might provide earlier undiscovered places or rulers; reconcile rather than overwrite. The creator may retcon or expand all newly created placements.
